newsitem.title: USA: High Court won't review Denver bond ruling appeal.
newsitem.headline: High Court won't review Denver bond ruling appeal.

text.p: The city of Denver lost another round in its two-year battle with holders of bonds issued to build Denver International Airport, which opened in February 1995 way behind schedule and above budget.
On Monday, the U.S. Supreme Court let stand an appeals court finding that allows bondholders to sue cities for damages under the federal securities laws.

The High Court's decision to not consider the November 1996 ruling by the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals means that the class-action lawsuit involving $3 billion of tax-exempt bonds to build the $5 billion airport can proceed.

The original lawsuit filed by investors charged that Denver knew, but failed to disclose, problems with a state-of-the-art baggage handling system that triggered an 18-month delay in the airport's opening and a downgrade of the bonds' ratings.

Denver moved to dismiss the case, saying that amendments to the securities laws passed by Congress in 1975 made clear that the Securities and Exchange Commission could sue municipalities for securities fraud violations, but did not explicitly say private entities could sue.
The appeals panel rejected the argument and Denver turned to the High Court for review of the issue.

The city warned in a recent brief that the appeals' court decision giving investors the right to sue municipal issuers "will have serious adverse effects on the ability of municipalities to use bonds to fund their capital needs."
But bondholders responded that subjecting municipalities to liability furthers the purpose of federal securities laws, which is to protect the investing public and deter wrongdoing.
